doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: European versus American appreciation of jazz
summary: Europeans appreciated jazz as an art form earlier; jazz is now heard more in concert than in clubs.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Did you notice a difference in playing over there? Because a number of people have talked about the difference in the way the music is accepted, or the artists, between the United States and Europe.

Well at that time it was quite noticeable. I’m not sure you could say — I think you could say it’s the same now. Europeans came to appreciate jazz as an art form earlier than, ironically, earlier than we did in America. They got into it in a scholarly way, and a critical way, earlier than anybody else did, with the exception of people like Leonard Feather perhaps. But even in the 20’s, the French were into jazz and Charles Delaunay was the first person to think of doing a discography of jazz recordings. That was in the early 30’s if I’m not mistaken.
It seems like sometimes the — something that comes from somewhere else has an exotic quality to it.
Just like we might listen to Russian folk music and think it’s really really artsy, where they think of it as everyday music.

That’s very true. I think the Europeans have always wanted to hear jazz in concert more or earlier than we ever did here. Of course another change that we’ve all witnesses is that now in general jazz is heard in concert, there are still jazz clubs, but there are many more jazz concerts. So that’s another strange twist of events.
